map.theme: A mountain observatory town of telescopes and measuring instruments, where an exam hall with ticking clocks, a tax office of tidy ledgers, a travel depot with departure boards, an insurance vault with balance scales and an auction square under a great bell are linked by stone steps. The palette is slate, lime and clean ivory, and the mood moves from careful checking at the exam hall to sharp-eyed confidence at the auction square.

scenarios.title: First Test Plan for the Vidya Vahini Exam Portal
scenarios.background: Vidya Vahini is a fictional online exam portal used by a state board in Karnataka for 200,000 students. A junior QA engineer joins two weeks before results go live. The registration form accepts applicants aged 18 to 60, results show a percentage calculated from marks, and developers complain that bug reports are vague, such as 'results page broken'. The QA lead asks her to design tests and write better reports.
constraints: Results go live in two weeks and cannot be delayed
There are two QA engineers for six developers
Wrong results would affect students' admissions

questions.prompt: The age field must accept applicants aged 18 to 60 inclusive. Which set of ages best tests the boundaries?

options.text: 25, 35 and 45, which are typical ages of real applicants
17, 18, 60 and 61, on and just outside each boundary
0 and 100, the most extreme values anyone might type
Every whole age from 1 to 100, checked one after another

questions.explanation: Bugs cluster at the edges of ranges, for example a developer writing 'greater than 18' instead of 'at least 18'. Testing the boundary values themselves and the values just outside them, 17, 18, 60 and 61, catches these off-by-one mistakes with very few tests.

why_others_wrong.a: Values in the middle of the range rarely reveal mistakes at the edges.
why_others_wrong.c: Extreme values check far outside the range but miss errors right at 18 and 60.
why_others_wrong.d: Testing every value is wasteful and still gives no more insight than the boundaries.

questions.key_justification: Boundary value analysis tests on and just beyond each edge of a valid range.

questions.prompt: Which bug report will help the developers most?

options.text: 'Results page broken. Please fix urgently, students are waiting.'
'The results feature does not work properly on the portal, sometimes.'
'I think the percentage maths is wrong. The developer should check it.'
Steps, expected 72.5% vs actual 7.25%, browser, roll no. and a screenshot

questions.explanation: A useful bug report lets a developer reproduce the problem without asking questions: the exact steps, the expected and actual results, the environment such as browser and test account, and evidence such as a screenshot. Here it also reveals the likely cause, a misplaced decimal point.

why_others_wrong.a: Urgency without details leaves the developer guessing what is broken and where.
why_others_wrong.b: 'Sometimes' and 'not properly' give no way to reproduce or locate the problem.
why_others_wrong.c: A suspicion with no steps or data cannot be confirmed or fixed.

questions.key_justification: Good bug reports give steps, expected versus actual results, environment and evidence.

questions.prompt: Which two checks are best written as unit tests?

options.text: The function that turns marks into a percentage
A browser journey from login all the way to results
The check that a roll number has the right format
A load test with 10,000 students checking results
An unscripted exploratory session on the results page

questions.explanation: Unit tests check small pieces of logic in isolation, quickly and many times, such as calculating a percentage or validating a roll number format. They can cover many input cases in milliseconds.

why_others_wrong.b: A full browser journey is an end-to-end test that crosses many components.
why_others_wrong.d: Load testing measures the whole system under traffic, not a single unit.
why_others_wrong.e: Exploratory testing is a manual, human-led activity, not an automated unit test.

questions.key_justification: Unit tests target small, isolated pieces of logic.

questions.prompt: Match each type of testing to its purpose.

targets.text: Confirm the system meets the business's requirements before sign-off
Quickly confirm a new build's key features work at all
Learn about the product and test it at once, without scripts
Check that existing features still work after a change

questions.explanation: A smoke test is a fast check that a build is not fundamentally broken before deeper testing. Regression tests protect existing behaviour after changes, exploratory testing uses a tester's skill to find unexpected problems, and acceptance testing confirms the system does what the business asked for.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Confusing smoke and regression testing: a smoke test is a quick, shallow check of key features, while regression testing is a broader check that nothing that used to work has broken.

questions.key_justification: Each testing type answers a different question about the build.

scenarios.title: Building the Automation Suite for Saral Tax
scenarios.background: Saral Tax is a fictional income-tax filing website from Pune used by 900,000 taxpayers. Manual regression testing of the main flows takes four days before every release. The QA team has been given time to build an automated test suite. The pages change often, the developers use generated CSS class names, the tax rules use income slabs and age groups, and the team must decide what to automate and how to structure the tests so they stay maintainable.
constraints: Taxpayers' real PAN and bank details must never appear in tests
The suite must keep working as pages are redesigned
tests_topics: Test design techniques and test data

questions.prompt: What should the team automate first?

options.text: Every screen in the product, including rarely used admin pages
Stable, high-value flows repeated each release, like filing
A brand-new page whose design will change again next week
A one-time data migration check that runs once and is retired

questions.explanation: Automation pays off where the same checks run every release and failures would be costly, such as logging in, filing a return and paying tax. Those flows are also fairly stable, so the tests will not need constant rewriting.

why_others_wrong.a: Automating everything at once spreads effort thin and includes low-value pages.
why_others_wrong.c: Tests for a page that keeps changing must be rewritten constantly.
why_others_wrong.d: A check that runs once gives no return on the effort of automating it.

questions.key_justification: Automate stable, high-value, frequently repeated checks first.

questions.prompt: Tests keep breaking because they find buttons by generated CSS classes like .btn-x7f2a or by XPath position. How should elements be located?

options.text: Use the full absolute XPath copied from the browser's DevTools
Find elements by their pixel coordinates on a fixed screen size
Use the generated CSS class names, but update them every release
Use dedicated test ids, or roles and labels that users see

questions.explanation: Attributes such as data-testid exist only for testing and do not change when the layout or styling is redesigned. Locating elements by their accessible role and visible label, such as the 'Submit return' button, also keeps tests close to how users find things.

why_others_wrong.a: Absolute XPaths break as soon as any element above the target moves.
why_others_wrong.b: Coordinates break with every screen size, font or layout change.
why_others_wrong.c: Updating selectors each release is the maintenance cost the team is trying to avoid.

questions.key_justification: Use stable, intention-revealing selectors rather than layout- or style-dependent ones.

questions.prompt: The login page's layout is about to change, and 120 tests interact with it. How should the suite be structured so the change is cheap?

options.text: Copy the login steps into each test so that tests are independent
Delete all the login tests and check the login page by hand instead
Put the login page's actions in one page object the tests all use
Record each test with a recorder tool and re-record any that break

questions.explanation: The page object pattern keeps each page's locators and actions, such as logIn(user), in one class. When the login page changes, only that class is updated, and all 120 tests keep working unchanged.

why_others_wrong.a: Copied steps mean 120 places to update when the page changes.
why_others_wrong.b: Manual checking brings back the slow, repetitive work automation was meant to remove.
why_others_wrong.d: Recorded tests are brittle and duplicate steps, so re-recording them becomes a constant chore.

questions.key_justification: Page objects centralise page details so UI changes are fixed in one place.

questions.prompt: Which two test-data practices should the suite follow?

options.text: Each test creates the data it needs, via the API, and cleans up
All tests share one taxpayer account, running at the same time
Use made-up taxpayers with fake PANs and fake bank details
Copy the production database, real taxpayer data and all
Rely on tests running in a fixed order to set up each other

questions.explanation: Tests that create and clean up their own data can run in any order and in parallel without interfering with each other. Synthetic taxpayers keep real personal and financial data out of test environments, where it is less protected.

why_others_wrong.b: Tests running at the same time on one account overwrite each other's data and fail randomly.
why_others_wrong.d: Real taxpayer data in test systems is a serious privacy and legal risk.
why_others_wrong.e: Order-dependent tests break when one fails or when the suite runs in parallel.

questions.key_justification: Tests should own their synthetic data and be independent of each other.

questions.prompt: Match each test design technique to an example from the tax rules.

targets.text: Test every combination of age group, residency and deductions
Test one income from inside each tax slab
Check returns move from draft to filed and block invalid moves
Test incomes exactly at each slab's limit and one rupee over

questions.explanation: Equivalence partitioning picks one value per group that should behave the same, such as one income per slab. Boundary value analysis targets the edges of those groups, decision tables cover combinations of conditions, and state transition testing checks allowed and forbidden moves between a return's states.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Mixing up partitioning and boundaries: partitioning tests one value from the middle of each group, while boundary analysis tests the edges where the groups meet.

questions.key_justification: Each technique reduces the test count while targeting a different kind of defect.

code_pool.prompt: Tax bugs hide at slab edges: an income exactly at a limit is taxed by the wrong slab. Boundary value analysis tests just below, at and just above every edge. The input is one line with the slab upper limits, in any order. Complete `boundary_values`: return 0 plus, for each limit b, the values b - 1, b and b + 1 (never below 0), each once and sorted. The program prints them on one line.
code_pool.explanation: Errors cluster at boundaries (a < written where <= was meant), so three values around each edge catch them with very few tests. A set removes overlaps when two limits are close, and sorting makes the list easy to review and to turn into a data-driven test.
code_pool.key_justification: Boundary value analysis: generate, de-duplicate and sort test inputs.

code_pool.prompt: An automated test needs an oracle: an independent way to know the right answer. Write the tax oracle for Saral Tax. The first line is n, then n slabs `limit rate` in increasing order (rate is a whole percent; the last limit is `inf`); then m, then m incomes in rupees. Complete `tax_due`: each slab taxes only the part of the income that falls inside it (this is not a flat rate on the whole income). Work in integers and round the tax down to whole rupees. The program prints `income tax` per income.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def tax_due(slabs, income):
    """slabs: (upper limit, rate %) in increasing order; the last limit is None (no upper limit). Each slab taxes only the part of the income inside it. Return the tax in whole rupees, rounded down."""
    # Write your code here.
    return 0


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    slabs = []
    for i in range(n):
        limit, rate = data[1 + i].split()
        slabs.append((None if limit == "inf" else int(limit), int(rate)))
    m = int(data[1 + n])
    for i in range(m):
        income = int(data[2 + n + i])
        print(income, tax_due(slabs, income))


main()
code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def tax_due(slabs, income):
    """slabs: (upper limit, rate %) in increasing order; the last limit is None (no upper limit). Each slab taxes only the part of the income inside it. Return the tax in whole rupees, rounded down."""
    paise, lower = 0, 0
    for limit, rate in slabs:
        upper = income if limit is None else min(income, limit)
        if upper > lower:
            paise += (upper - lower) * rate        # rupees x percent = paise
        if limit is None or income <= limit:
            break
        lower = limit
    return paise // 100


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    slabs = []
    for i in range(n):
        limit, rate = data[1 + i].split()
        slabs.append((None if limit == "inf" else int(limit), int(rate)))
    m = int(data[1 + n])
    for i in range(m):
        income = int(data[2 + n + i])
        print(income, tax_due(slabs, income))


main()
code_pool.explanation: Walking the slabs in order and taxing only the slice inside each one is progressive taxation; rupees x percent is exactly paise, so integer arithmetic avoids rounding drift. A test suite then compares the website's answer for the boundary incomes with this oracle.
code_pool.key_justification: Slab-wise accumulation over an ordered array (a test oracle).

scenarios.title: Taming Flaky Tests at Ghumakkad Travels
scenarios.background: Ghumakkad Travels is a fictional holiday-booking site in Chandigarh with 1,400 automated UI and API tests. The team no longer trusts the suite: tests fail at random with 'element not found', some pass alone but fail in the full run, a date test fails only when the CI server runs in the early hours, and a payment bug reached Safari users even though every test passed. The QA lead has a week to make the suite trustworthy again.
constraints: The CI server runs in UTC, while the business runs on Indian time
The suite runs in parallel on four workers
Many customers book on iPhones using Safari

questions.prompt: Search tests fail at random with 'element not found'. Results load asynchronously, and the tests use sleep(2) before checking them. What is the fix?

options.text: Increase every sleep from 2 seconds to 10 seconds across the suite
Wait for the specific condition, such as the results being visible
Rerun each failing test automatically, up to five times in a row
Remove the result checks so the search tests can no longer fail

questions.explanation: A fixed sleep is either too short on a slow run or wasted time on a fast one. Waiting explicitly until a condition is true, such as the results list being visible or the search request finishing, makes the test as fast as the app and reliable when it is slow.

why_others_wrong.a: Longer sleeps make the suite much slower and still fail when loading takes longer than 10 seconds.
why_others_wrong.c: Retries hide the timing problem instead of fixing it.
why_others_wrong.d: Without checks the tests pass but verify nothing.

questions.key_justification: Replace fixed sleeps with explicit waits for the condition the test needs.

questions.prompt: Some tests pass when run alone but fail in the full parallel run. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: The CI machines are too slow to run tests one at a time on
Tests share state, like one account or cart, and interfere
The tests were written in the wrong programming language
The test names are too long for the test runner to handle

questions.explanation: Passing alone but failing together is the classic sign of tests depending on shared state: one test changes a shared account, cart or database row that another relies on. Giving each test its own data and resetting state between tests removes the interference.

why_others_wrong.a: Slowness would affect tests run alone too, not only the combined run.
why_others_wrong.c: The language does not explain failures that depend on which tests run together.
why_others_wrong.d: Name length does not affect whether tests interfere with each other.

questions.key_justification: Order- or concurrency-dependent failures point to shared state between tests.

questions.prompt: Every test passed, but a payment bug reached Safari users. The suite runs only on Chrome. What should change?

options.text: Tell customers to switch to Chrome for booking their holidays
Add more Chrome tests for the payment page and its flows
Run the critical flows like payment on WebKit/Safari too
Run the entire suite on every browser for every commit

questions.explanation: Browsers differ in their engines, so a flow that works in Chrome can fail in Safari. Running the most important journeys, such as search, booking and payment, on WebKit or real Safari as well as Chrome covers the browsers many customers actually use, without multiplying the whole suite.

why_others_wrong.a: Customers will not change browsers, and the site must work for them.
why_others_wrong.b: More Chrome tests still never run Safari's engine.
why_others_wrong.d: Running all 1,400 tests on every browser for every commit is slow and costly; critical flows give most of the value.

questions.key_justification: Cover critical flows on the browsers your users actually use.

questions.prompt: A test that checks 'today's bookings' fails only when CI runs between midnight and 5:30 am Indian time. Which two fixes address the cause?

options.text: Have the test control the clock with a fixed date and time zone
Run the test suite only during office hours to avoid the window
Work out 'today' in the same time zone the application uses
Delete the date checks from this test so it can always pass
Rerun the test each night until it eventually passes again

questions.explanation: Between midnight and 5:30 am in India it is still the previous day in UTC, so a test that works out 'today' on the UTC server disagrees with the app, which uses Indian time. Fixing the clock and time zone in the test, and calculating dates in the app's own time zone, removes the dependence on when the test runs.

why_others_wrong.b: Avoiding the time window hides a real time-zone bug that customers may also hit.
why_others_wrong.d: Removing the checks means the test no longer verifies the feature.
why_others_wrong.e: Reruns at the same time of night fail the same way.

questions.key_justification: Tests must control time and use the same time zone as the application.

questions.prompt: Match each failure to its most likely cause.

items.text: Clicks fail with 'element click intercepted by another element'
A test stays green even though the feature it covers is broken
API tests start failing with 401 an hour into the suite
Screenshot comparisons fail on every single run by a few pixels

targets.text: The test never asserts the outcome that actually matters
The screen includes changing content such as live timestamps
A cookie banner or overlay is covering the target button
The auth token expires partway through the test run

questions.explanation: An intercepted click means something is on top of the button, often a banner or modal. A test that passes while the feature is broken is not checking the right result, 401s after a fixed time point to an expiring token, and screenshots that never match usually contain content that changes on every run.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Treating the always-green test as healthy: a test that cannot fail gives false confidence, so its assertions must be checked by deliberately breaking the feature.

questions.key_justification: Each failure pattern points to a specific test or environment cause.

code_pool.prompt: 1,400 tests fail in so many slightly different ways that nobody reads the failures any more. Group them. The first line is n, then n failure messages. Complete `group_failures`: replace every quoted part ('...' or "...") with S, then every run of digits with N, so `Timeout after 3000 ms` and `Timeout after 5000 ms` become the same. The program prints `count message` for each distinct normalised message, most frequent first, ties by message.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def group_failures(messages):
    """Normalise each failure message: replace every part in single or double quotes with S, then every run of digits with N. Return [(count, normalised message)] for each distinct one, most frequent first, ties by message."""
    # Write your code here.
    return [(1, m) for m in messages]


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    for count, message in group_failures(data[1:1 + n]):
        print(count, message)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Replacing the parts that change between runs (numbers, quoted values) leaves the shape of each failure, and counting shapes turns 1,400 red lines into a handful of distinct problems. Quotes go first so a date inside quotes becomes one S, not several N.
code_pool.key_justification: Normalise strings with patterns, then count by shape.

code_pool.prompt: Some tests pass alone but fail in the full run because they quietly rely on data another test left behind. Find those hidden dependencies. The first line is n, then n steps in run order, `test READ key` or `test WRITE key`. Complete `hidden_dependencies`: a test depends on another when it READs a key whose latest write came from a different test, and it has not written that key itself earlier. The program prints each distinct `reader <- writer key`, sorted, or ISOLATED.
code_pool.starter_code:
import sys


def hidden_dependencies(steps):
    """steps: (test, READ or WRITE, key) in run order. A test depends on another when it READs a key whose latest write came from a different test and it has not written that key itself earlier. Return the distinct (reader, writer, key) triples, sorted."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    steps = [tuple(data[1 + i].split()) for i in range(n)]
    pairs = hidden_dependencies(steps)
    if not pairs:
        print("ISOLATED")
    for reader, writer, key in pairs:
        print(reader, "<-", writer, key)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Tracking the last writer of each key in a dictionary while replaying the run shows exactly which test reads another test's data. Each such pair is an isolation bug: the fix is for the reader to create its own data (a fixture), so tests pass in any order and in parallel.
code_pool.key_justification: Replay steps with a last-writer map to find order dependencies.

scenarios.title: Testing What Matters at Jeevan Raksha Insurance
scenarios.background: Jeevan Raksha is a fictional insurance company in Chennai whose platform is made of eight microservices for quotes, policies, payments and claims. Management has demanded 90% code coverage. The end-to-end suite across all eight services takes three hours and fails randomly. A release is due in two days with less testing time than usual, and three known minor bugs are still open. The QA lead must decide where to spend effort and how to advise on the release.
constraints: Payment and policy issuing errors cost money and trust
Eight teams deploy their services independently
Only two days remain before the planned release

questions.prompt: There is less testing time than usual before the release. How should the QA lead decide what to test?

options.text: Test every feature equally lightly, so that nothing is skipped
Test only the features that are easiest and quickest to check
Focus on high-impact, high-risk areas like payments, and changes
Test only the parts the developers say they are worried about

questions.explanation: Risk-based testing ranks areas by how bad a failure would be and how likely it is. Payments and policy issuing carry the highest impact, and recently changed code is the most likely to break, so the limited time goes there first.

why_others_wrong.a: Spreading effort evenly leaves the riskiest flows under-tested.
why_others_wrong.b: Easy checks are rarely where the dangerous bugs are.
why_others_wrong.d: Developers' worries are useful input, but they are not a complete risk assessment.

questions.key_justification: Prioritise testing by impact and likelihood of failure.

questions.prompt: Management demands 90% code coverage. What should the QA lead explain about coverage?

options.text: It is a full measure of quality, so 90% coverage means 90% bug-free
It shows which code ran, not which behaviour was actually checked
It can only be measured accurately for frontend code, not services
It should be pushed to 100% at any cost before the next release

questions.explanation: Coverage counts which lines were executed, so a test can run code without asserting anything useful. It is valuable for finding untested areas, while the quality of assertions, checked for example with mutation testing, shows whether tests would actually catch bugs.

why_others_wrong.a: High coverage with weak assertions can still let serious bugs through.
why_others_wrong.c: Coverage tools exist for backend services as well as front-end code.
why_others_wrong.d: Chasing 100% often produces low-value tests written only to hit the number.

questions.key_justification: Coverage shows what code ran, not whether behaviour was verified.

questions.prompt: The three-hour end-to-end suite across eight services is slow and flaky, and teams deploy independently. What should replace most of it?

options.text: Consumer-driven contract tests, plus a few end-to-end journeys
An even larger end-to-end suite, run once a week on weekends
Manual regression testing of all eight services before releases
No integration testing at all, only unit tests in each service

questions.explanation: Contract tests check that each service provides exactly what its consumers expect, and they run quickly within each team's own pipeline whenever that service changes. A small number of end-to-end tests then covers the most critical journeys, such as buying a policy.

why_others_wrong.b: A bigger, weekly suite gives even slower feedback and stays flaky.
why_others_wrong.c: Manual testing of eight independently deployed services cannot keep pace.
why_others_wrong.d: Unit tests alone miss mismatches between services, which are a major source of failures.

questions.key_justification: Contract tests verify service integrations quickly; keep only a few end-to-end tests.

questions.prompt: Three minor known bugs remain open before the release. Which two practices should guide the decision?

options.text: QA lays out each bug's severity, impact and workaround
QA blocks any release that still has an open bug of any kind
Decide against release criteria that were agreed in advance
Hide the open bugs from management so the date is still met
Release without telling the support team about the open bugs

questions.explanation: QA's role is to give a clear picture of risk: how severe each bug is, who it affects and whether there is a workaround. Comparing that with exit criteria agreed before testing began, such as no open critical or high bugs, makes the release decision objective rather than a last-minute argument.

why_others_wrong.b: Almost every release has some minor known bugs; blocking on any bug means never shipping.
why_others_wrong.d: Hiding bugs removes the information decision-makers need.
why_others_wrong.e: Support needs to know about known issues to help customers quickly.

questions.key_justification: Inform release decisions with transparent risk and agreed exit criteria.

code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def plan_tests(features, budget):
    """features: (name, likelihood 1-5, impact 1-5, minutes to test). Risk = likelihood x impact. Go through the features by risk high to low (ties: fewer minutes, then name) and test each one that still fits the remaining minutes. Return (names chosen in that order, risk covered, total risk, minutes used)."""
    ranked = sorted(features, key=lambda f: (-f[1] * f[2], f[3], f[0]))
    left, covered, chosen = budget, 0, []
    for name, likelihood, impact, minutes in ranked:
        if minutes <= left:                 # skip what doesn't fit, keep going
            left -= minutes
            covered += likelihood * impact
            chosen.append(name)
    total = sum(l * i for _, l, i, _ in features)
    return chosen, covered, total, budget - left


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    budget = int(data[0])
    n = int(data[1])
    features = []
    for i in range(n):
        name, likelihood, impact, minutes = data[2 + i].split()
        features.append((name, int(likelihood), int(impact), int(minutes)))
    chosen, covered, total, used = plan_tests(features, budget)
    for name in chosen:
        print("test", name)
    print("covered_risk", covered, "of", total)
    print("minutes_used", used)


main()
code_pool.explanation: Ranking by likelihood x impact and filling the time greedily puts testing where a failure would hurt most. Reporting covered risk out of total risk makes the trade-off explicit for the release decision, which is more honest than a coverage percentage.
code_pool.key_justification: Rank by a risk score, then greedily fill a time budget.

code_pool.prompt: The end-to-end suite across eight services is slow and flaky. Contract tests check each service's response shape on its own instead. The first line is n, then n contract lines `path type` (a dotted path through objects; type one of string, number, boolean, object, array, null), then one line of JSON: the provider's response. Complete `verify`: report `missing PATH` if the path does not exist, or `type PATH expected=T got=U` if the value has the wrong type (true and false are boolean, never number), in contract order. The program prints the problems, or PASS.
code_pool.starter_code:
import json
import sys


def verify(contract, response):
    """contract: (dotted path, type) with type one of string, number, boolean, object, array, null. response: parsed JSON. Follow each path through objects. Return, in contract order, 'missing PATH' or 'type PATH expected=T got=U'. true/false are boolean, never number."""
    # Write your code here.
    return []


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    contract = [tuple(data[1 + i].split()) for i in range(n)]
    response = json.loads(data[1 + n])
    problems = verify(contract, response)
    print("\n".join(problems) if problems else "PASS")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Walking each dotted path through nested dictionaries and comparing JSON types is the core of consumer-driven contract testing: it fails fast, in seconds, when a provider changes a field, without starting all eight services. The bool-before-number check matters because Python treats True as the integer 1.
code_pool.key_justification: Navigate nested maps by path and check JSON types.

scenarios.title: Test Strategy for the Digital Mandi Launch
scenarios.background: Digital Mandi is a fictional online auction platform from Indore where farmers sell produce to traders across India. At closing time, up to 50,000 traders bid in the final minute. Traders link bank accounts, many use the mobile app on slow networks, and some farmers rely on screen readers. The company is moving from testing at the end of each release to building quality in from the start, and the QA lead must design the strategy for launch.
constraints: Auctions close with up to 50,000 bids in the last minute
Traders' bank details must never be visible to others
The app must work on slow 2G and 3G connections

questions.prompt: Put QA's activities within one sprint in order.

options.text: Automate the tests alongside the feature's development
Review the story and agree testable acceptance criteria
Run exploratory testing on the finished feature before release
Run the automated tests in CI on every change
Design the test cases and the test data they need

questions.explanation: QA starts by making the requirement testable, then designs cases and data from it. Tests are automated while the feature is built and run in CI on every change, and exploratory testing of the finished feature catches what scripts did not anticipate before it ships.

why_others_wrong.common_mistake: Writing automated tests only after the feature is finished, which pushes testing to the end of the sprint and delays feedback to developers.

questions.key_justification: Define criteria, design tests, automate alongside development, run in CI, then explore.

questions.prompt: How should the team test the final minute of an auction with 50,000 bidders?

options.text: Ask ten colleagues to bid at the same moment from their phones
Test on a developer laptop with one simulated bidder at a time
Wait to see how the real launch-day auction performs, then fix it
Ramp realistic load and spikes to peak in a production-like setup

questions.explanation: A load test with realistic bidding patterns, ramping up to the expected peak plus a sudden spike, shows how the system behaves where it matters. Running it in a production-like environment and measuring 95th-percentile response times and error rates shows whether bids are accepted in time.

why_others_wrong.a: Ten people are thousands of times below the real load.
why_others_wrong.b: One bidder at a time tests nothing about concurrency.
why_others_wrong.c: Finding the limit on launch day means real farmers and traders lose auctions.

questions.key_justification: Performance testing needs realistic peak and spike load in a production-like environment.

questions.prompt: The company wants to 'shift testing left'. What does that look like in practice?

options.text: QA helps refine stories into testable Given-When-Then criteria
QA tests everything in a longer phase just before each release
Developers stop testing so that QA owns all quality on their own
Testing moves to after release, guided by customer complaints

why_others_wrong.c: Shift-left spreads quality across the team rather than putting it on QA alone.
why_others_wrong.d: Testing after release moves it right, to the most expensive point.

code_pool.reference_solution:
import sys


def load_summary(requests):
    """requests: (time in ms since the test started, HTTP status). Group by whole second (time // 1000). Return (the most requests in one second, that second (the earliest on a tie), number of responses with status 500 or above)."""
    per_second, errors = {}, 0
    for t, status in requests:
        per_second[t // 1000] = per_second.get(t // 1000, 0) + 1
        errors += status >= 500                 # 429 is throttling, not a server error
    second = min(per_second, key=lambda s: (-per_second[s], s))
    return per_second[second], second, errors


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split("\n")
    n = int(data[0])
    requests = [tuple(map(int, data[1 + i].split())) for i in range(n)]
    peak, second, errors = load_summary(requests)
    print("peak_rps", peak, "at second", second)
    print("error_rate", f"{100 * errors / n:.2f}%")
    print("verdict", "PASS" if errors * 100 <= n else "FAIL")


main()
code_pool.explanation: Bucketing timestamps by second in a dictionary gives the throughput curve, and its peak is what the auction must survive at closing time. Counting only 5xx as errors keeps deliberate throttling (429) separate from real failures; the pass rule is an integer check, not a float.
code_pool.key_justification: Bucket events by time in a hash map; summarise peak and errors.

The first line is `service sla n` (ms per bid, the acceptable wait in ms, number of bids), the second has the n arrival times in ms, in order. Complete `bid_queue`: the worker takes bids first come, first served, each for `service` ms; a bid waits from its arrival until the worker starts it. The program prints `max_wait`, `over_sla` (bids that waited longer than the SLA) and `last_finish`.

import sys


def bid_queue(arrivals, service, sla):

    print("over_sla", over)
    print("last_finish", finish)

code_pool.reference_solution:
from collections import deque
import sys


def bid_queue(arrivals, service, sla):
    """arrivals: bid times in ms, in order. One worker handles bids first come, first served; each takes `service` ms. A bid waits from its arrival until the worker starts it. Return (longest wait, number of bids that waited more than `sla` ms, time the last bid finishes)."""
    queue = deque(arrivals)
    free_at = worst = over = 0
    while queue:
        arrived = queue.popleft()               # first come, first served
        start = max(arrived, free_at)
        wait = start - arrived
        worst = max(worst, wait)
        over += wait > sla
        free_at = start + service
    return worst, over, free_at


def main():
    data = sys.stdin.read().split()
    service, sla, n = int(data[0]), int(data[1]), int(data[2])
    arrivals = list(map(int, data[3:3 + n]))
    worst, over, finish = bid_queue(arrivals, service, sla)
    print("max_wait", worst)
    print("over_sla", over)
    print("last_finish", finish)


main()
code_pool.explanation: A FIFO queue with one server is the simplest performance model: each bid starts when it arrives or when the worker frees up, whichever is later. When arrivals come faster than service, waits grow without limit; the model shows how many workers (or how much faster processing) the final minute needs before any load test is run.
